chunks: And as for what Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Al-Nadr from 'Asim from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who frees a slave for the expiation of an oath or for dhihar; to whom does the walayah (manumission bond) belong? He said: 'To the one who frees him.'

Therefore, this report is understood to mean that the walayah belongs to him if the manumission bond transfers to him after the freeing, because if it does not transfer to him afterwards, it becomes sa'ibah, according to what we have previously mentioned in the first report.

key_terms.الْوَلَاءُ: Walayah: The bond of manumission, indicating the right of ownership and kinship between the freedman and his master.
key_terms.سَائِبَةً: Sa'ibah: A specific legal category of a freed slave whose walayah belongs to the public treasury or a specific entity depending on the school, often resulting when the specific bond does not transfer to the freer.
key_terms.ظِهَارٌ: Dhihar: A pre-Islamic and early Islamic form of divorce where a husband likens his wife to his mother's back.
key_terms.كَفَّارَةِ يَمِينٍ: Kaffarat yamin: Expiation for breaking an oath, which can involve freeing a slave.

ai.seo_question: Who owns the walayah when a slave is freed for expiation of an oath?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id to clarify the specific legal status of a slave manumitted for expiation (kaffarah), ruling that the manumitter retains the right of walayah. The text further elucidates that if the bond does not transfer to the manumitter, the slave falls into the category of sa'ibah, a concept rooted in pre-Islamic and early Islamic jurisprudence regarding those freed without a master. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise ownership rights in manumission transactions.
